video_title: Alcohol, Hangovers & How to Cure a Hangover Based on Science | Dr. Andrew Huberman
content: for those who get horrendous headaches after drinking try this. obviously a hangover is/can be a mixture of headache, tiredness, hanxiety and bad stomach. luckily i've never had a bad stomach from a hangover and all it makes me do is wanna eat more. i can mentally put up with any hanxiety and tiredness is not the end of the world. but i have always suffered from horrendous headaches when drinking. and i love a good drink. over the years i had just put up with the headaches as a sacrifice worth making for the enjoyment of a great night out. but a about a year ago i started questioning why i got such horrendous headaches from drinking when some of my pals seemed to get away with it. i went on line and researched headaches from drinking and everything said that it was from dehydration and losing essential salts and electrolytes from your system as your body urinates all the alcohol out as fast as possible as it sees it as a poison. the dehydrated causes your brain to swell and that's what causes the headaches. well how can i combat that i thought? these fizzy rehydration tablets seemed to suggest they were great at replacing all the salts and electrolytes. and for swelling anti inflammatory medication is what's usually took. so i gave it a go. and what i find is if i know i'm gonna be drinking a lot on say a saturday night, i take a hydration tablet when i get up in the morning. just before i go out i take a couple of ibuprofen tablets. i put some by my bed with a glass of water and some hydration tablets too. when i get in at silly o clock in the morning i neck a pint of water with another hydration tablet and two more ibuprofen. when i wake up in the morning if i've followed this regime i swear, the difference between that and not doing it is chalk and cheese. i go from feeling like death warmed up to just quite tired. i neck another pint of water with a fizzy hydration tablet and two ibuprofen when i wake up and that sees me through for the rest of the day. instead of a debilitating hangover which leaves me unable to do anything but sit still on the sofa watching tv, i can pretty much function as would normally if id say was feeling like i needed to catch up on some sleep. i even make it to the gym sometimes now too. it might not work for everyone but if headaches are crippling for you after a night out partying hard try it.

video_title: Man Shares End of Life Realities After Terminal Cancer Diagnosis
content: tanner martin, a 25-year-old diagnosed with stage 4 colon cancer in 2020, shares his journey alongside his wife, shay wright. initially, tanner experienced digestive issues and blood in his stool, which he and doctors attributed to benign causes. medication temporarily alleviated symptoms, but they returned severely six months later, accompanied by fatigue. a colonoscopy revealed a large tumor blocking his colon, leading to a stage 4 diagnosis with metastases to his liver. despite aggressive treatments—12 rounds of folfox chemotherapy, 20 rounds of folfiri, 50 rounds of radiation, multiple surgeries, and smaller procedures—the cancer was deemed incurable in 2023. tanner also battled sepsis from june 2023 to january 2024, requiring extensive hospitalization and halting cancer treatment. the ordeal caused significant weight loss (100 pounds) and physical decline. facing a terminal diagnosis with a 14% five-year survival rate, tanner and shay focus on living fully, traveling to italy and ireland, adopting a cancer support dog, visiting disney world, and meeting mark hamill through the dream foundation. they held a "living funeral" to celebrate tanner’s life, planned end-of-life details (e.g., $23,000 funeral costs), and share their story on social media to process grief and raise awareness. tanner, a therapist with a master’s in marriage and family therapy, emphasizes early screening, noting the rising incidence of colorectal cancer in young people (including 11-year-olds in his support group). he advocates for life insurance and proactive health checks, having inspired others to get colonoscopies that detected precancerous conditions. tanner’s legacy is to encourage preparation for worst-case scenarios and living life fully despite fear.

video_title: What is Schizoaffective Disorder- Is It Worse Than Bipolar Disorder?
content: i was diagnosed almost 11 years ago. there are periods of my life when i think very clearly and feel contented. over the last several years, i have been anxious, stressed and isolated with seemingly no reprieve. i have been taking the same medication since the beginning and i wonder sometimes whether i am gaining anything from it other than weight and drowsiness. the path forward continues to be challenging and uncertain. i just try to give myself the grace occasionally that i feel poorly for a reason and much of it is out of my control. there have been benefits. i am a more peaceful person and i don’t drink anymore. sometimes the struggle just seems insurmountable. i see a therapist and have learned some coping strategies which can be effective. if you have just learned that you have schizoaffective disorder, i encourage you to take your medication, get plenty of sleep and try to afford yourself your feelings with the understanding that you can’t always be happy. it is possible to function in society and to be a positive presence in the lives of your close relations and cohort. it isn’t always easy but it comes with the territory. remember as well that anti-psychotics and alcohol don’t mix well. if you have a drink before you take your pills, you’ll probably sleep until mid afternoon the next day.

video_title: What It’s Like To Lose Someone To Suicide
content: warning to anyone who wants to engage in this comments section with any sincerity: a certain user has been posting here for months now, spreading very harmful rhetoric to people who are already hurting. they've been blaming grieving people for their loved one's suicide--"you didn't really care, or they'd still be here"--while also telling those thinking about ending their life that they are totally right in thinking no one cares about them, that these uncaring people are to blame for their pain, and that life offers no way out of the pain but death. even that dying would serve to punish those uncaring people, more or less the hannah baker philosophy--which was proven to literally lead to a spike in teen suicides when 13 reasons why came out. this user is even tearing down people trying to be supportive and uplifting to the suicidal, accusing them of being fake and countering their words with the "truth" of how actually, it's all hopeless and, on mass, no one cares. while also sometimes stopping to police the hurting people's grammar as they bare their souls, because why not. please don't take their dismal words to heart, nor try to be combative in turn. they appear to be deeply unhappy and bitter, and projecting that onto many people who do not deserve nor benefit from it. maybe they feel it as some sort of catharsis, or like they are "spreading awareness" or calling out an evil; but put all together, it amounts to urging already vulnerable, possibly quite isolated and lonely people to give up and die, and telling grieving people not to grieve because it's their fault for being horrible people. these are not things you'd tell someone you loved, nor even a stranger. it only kicks people while they're down. the causes of suicide cannot be reduced down to a sweeping "no one cared enough or they wouldn't have died." there are many paths to despair, and factors that even the most loving parents or supportive friends cannot fully control or even know about. i think if you kneejerk reduce all these deaths down to a single cause that neatly blames one party for everything, you are likely projecting from your own wounds. or else, are looking to manage your terror: after all, it's terrifying to think you could love someone dearly and do everything right, and yet be blindsided by this. it's easier to think it's only something that would happen if you'd made some horrible mistake, and then to think, of course, you would never make that mistake, so you're in the clear. it's a comforting thought at first, provides a sense of control--but when it's used to attack others, it becomes a poisonous one. if i am right, then it's all from pain and fear, so we can't judge too harsh--but still, it's very important to get a hold on. last thing we need is to hurt each other over this. at the same time, there is a real tiredness here. people in pain have often heard it all. "think of everyone who'd miss you." "reach out to someone." "there's help, you're not alone." "you are worthy to live." and for one reason or another, it seems to ring hollow. i don't have any easy answers for that. i might recommend the poem, "the view from halfway down." or to find those who felt the same as you, but lived to reach the other side of it, and see what they did to get there. or something like that. all i can say for sure is: i cared, at least enough to post this comment.

content: this entire video is such a red herring so let’s break it down: - public transit is often dirty, poorly maintained, and unreliable. we aren’t living in tokyo where the train arrives at 8:17:00 and a delay of 60 or more seconds results in fines. often, relying on public transit means that a person is sacrificing an incredible amount of time just…waiting. also, i don’t know about you, but i generally prefer that my morning commute not be permeated with the fragrance of eau d’urine. - high-cost neighborhoods are often quieter, better maintained, more visually appealing, and — mostly importantly — have better funded school districts. ignoring your third point for a moment, if an individual wanted their child to have access to the best possible public school education, they almost *have* to live in a high-cost housing area. that aside, though, you typically won’t find high-income communities that are riddled with trash and litter, have people coming and going at all hours of the night, or generally have disturbances. given that almost all of the residents of such neighborhoods are working professionals with 9-5 jobs, they not only tend to be quieter, but also seem to maintain their space better, since they had to work so hard to achieve it. - sending a child to private versus public school has little to do with classism and a whole lot to do with the quality of education that child will receive. we’re living in an era where americans’ functional literacy rates are the lowest they’ve been in decades. the standards for standardized tests have had to be lowered because so many students nation-wide are at risk of failing. i don’t want my child to be in an educational environment where the expectation is that (s)he will barely scrape by — i want him/her to be in an environment where (s)he will be challenged to succeed, where the students have more access to 1:1 learning and mentorship from teachers, and where the school isn’t struggling to fund basic programs. i can’t get that at the vast majority of public schools. - summer camp is a boon to working parents. children who aren’t old enough to stay home by themselves need to be looked after, and parents who don’t have the luxury to stop working for three months are often left with the choice of either (1) babysitters or (2) summer camp. between these two, summer camp is actually the more economical option. again, this has little to do with classism and almost everything to do with the practical necessity of needing to work while your child is off school. the fact is that most people who acquire disposable income aren’t trying to get away from “poor people,” they’re trying to get away from people and environments that are messy, dirty, loud, rude, ignorant, and inconsiderate. not *all* low-income communities are that way. not *all* high-income communities are spared those characterizations. but if you try to deny the reality of that trend, you’re living in willful ignorance.

content: ok i’m commenting this before watching the video as a proof that i have my own opinion on this release. i listened to it. it’s more diverse, yet still somehow boring. constipation slam. maybe it’s the same bpm, or it doesn’t groove for some reason. it sounds too…. even? at this point i’m genuinely interested what makes it boring. maybe it’s compressed too much? apart from that, some points: 1. why should i listen to the breakdown from thrones of blood and the riffs from voracious contempt if i can listen to pierced from within and voracious contempt? 2. it sounds like death metal spoken word. not a very good one at that. i prefer good music who happens to be political to political statement disguised as “music”. 3. kevin, you can’t do schoenberg, you’re not lille gruber. do schoenberg when you learn to do schuldiner or something. and also those clean sections - bro, no. 4. i found no disgorge influence on this record. some tremolo though, okay great 5. one positive thing i can say is that this no longer feels like a beatdown hardcore album pretending to be slam. progress! now make it good (death) metal. 6. the voivod track at the end is okay. sometimes cringe, but i appreciate branching out. still, something’s up with the sound. 7. acts 2 and 3 are pisstakes. 8. i thought xander bridge played for torture and it would rub off in a positive way on this release. turns out it didn’t and it was a different xander. no offence to the other xander. maybe when kevin makes a truly good album we’ll stop talking about him. i dunno. maybe he’s doing it right. i won’t return to it though.

(i just got goosebumps thinking of this again). please, if this is you and you are going through this, please know that what you have ahead of you is beautiful. the pain you will feel and the fears you will face will only be temporary and will be well worth it. you will always be with your loved ones in blood and heart and with their memories. video_title: Why is it so hard to escape poverty? - Ann-Helén Bay
content: why is it so hard to escape poverty? this video does something important. it dismantles the myth that poverty is simply about motivation or effort. instead, it explains the poverty trap, how benefit cliffs, unstable wages, rising costs, and rigid eligibility rules actually punish progress. people can lose healthcare, childcare, food assistance, or housing supports the moment they earn slightly more, even when that income is still not enough to survive. so, working harder can literally make life worse. the animation makes it simple, but the message is heavy; systems built without flexibility create cycles that are incredibly hard to escape. what struck me most-especially reading the comments is how many people share the same lived experience: afraid to accept a raise losing benefits overnight choosing between medical care and rent working full time and still going hungry that's not individual failure, that structural design. the video also highlights what does help: gradual befit phase-outs, access to childcare, healthcare continuity, education, transportation, and policies that support upward mobility instead of penalizing it. this reinforces why we don't just help people cope - we advocate to change the systems themselves. poverty isn't a character flaw. it is a policy outcome. powerful, compassionate. and absolutely worth watching.

card,” a separate third‑degree felony if value obtained exceeds 100 in six months. ​ he will be charged as an adult (18 is adult under florida criminal law; there is no juvenile treatment here). this money taken). ​ what usually happens for 1st‑time offenders many first‑time, non‑violent, third‑degree felony theft defendants receive probation, restitution, and possibly county jail rather than a full 5‑year prison term, especially if they accept a plea. however, employee theft is often treated as a “breach of trust,” so prosecutors and judges can be less lenient than with shoplifting from a random store. a withhold of adjudication or entry into a diversion/pretrial intervention program is sometimes possible, which can avoid a formal felony conviction if successfully completed (very fact‑ and county‑specific). many defense firms describe this as a common goal in first‑offender theft cases. long‑term consequences a felony theft or fraud conviction creates a permanent criminal record exposure to multiple third‑degree felonies (grand theft plus possible credit‑card fraud), each carrying up to 5 years, gives the state significant leverage. felony theft/fraud record can follow him for life in background checks, making future employment—especially in retail, finance, and customer‑facing roles—much harder. loss of job, damaged reputation, financial burden of restitution, court costs, and supervision fees are all likely negative outcomes.

content: okay, the story of robert johnson being a hugely influentual musician among black musicians in the 1930s-1950s is completely false. he was a truly great musician, and a couple of delta blues musicians knew him, but in that world he was essentially a one-hit wonder, the only record he made that sold any number of copies was terraplane blues, and “successful in delta blues circles” was nowhere near the level of actually successful records, and his later recordings had basically no success at all. in the words of a biographer, elijah wald, “knowing about robert johnson and muddy waters, but not dinah washington and leroy carr was like knowing about the sir douglas quintet but not the beatles.” additionally, the kind of guitar-based blues music that robert johnson made wasn’t actually all that influential on early ‘50s rock and roll, if you look at rnb-derived rock and roll music from that period, aside from chuck berry and bo diddley, it’s dominated by piano and sax, being derived from swing-based jump blues musicians like louis jordan, which ultimately came from bessie smith-style vaudevillian blues. (if you want to attribute rock and roll to one man, for the record, attribute it to louis jordan), new orleans piano playing, and general boogie woogie music from the previous decade. not to say that johnson wasn’t influential, he was, but rather, he was influential on white musicians in the ‘60s, mainly due to the influence of john hammond, one of the few white people to have even registered johnson’s existence while he was still alive. he had tried to get johnson onto the 1938/1939 “from spirituals to swing” concerts, but was disappointed to find he’d died. in 1961 he put out the album “king of the delta blues singers”, and almost all of robert johnson’s current reputation comes from that album, which eventually became widely popular with people who were “in” as it were (it’s in the backgroind of the cover of bob dylan’s “bringing it all back home”, just as an example), and this turned hin into a totemic figure among white blues fans. the story about him selling his soul to the devil at a crossroads was actually originally said about the different blues musician tommy johnson, who liked to create a spooky aura around himself. it was attributed to robert because of the similarity in the name, references to satan and crossroads in various of robert’s songs, as well as a story told by son house of robert challenging him to a guitar duel and failing badly, and then coming back later much better. (the actual truth, where johnson spend some time training under a much more experienced musician, and got better, is less well known) most of this rant was from information from the excellent rock music history podcast “a history of rock music in 500 songs”, if you want to learn more about ‘50s rock and robert johnson, that’s a good place to start ( johnson is covered in the episode about cream and the song crossroads blues)

munitions into ships. there was also some mention of the mutiny that was subsequently prosecuted. i wish i could recall more than just general knowledge type of information about who was responsible for placing the signage and what was actually reported on the signs. but, fifty years have faded the memory too much for me to recall the details. still, when i read the title you applied to this video, i was immediately convinced you must have been referring to port chicago. i object to your statement that the port chicago disaster started the civil rights movement. the naacp was founded in 1909 and thurgood marshall (who figured prominently in your re-telling of the events) litigated his first case for the naacp in 1935, having to do with a black gentleman's experience of being denied admission to the u. of maryland law school on account of his race. marshall argued that the state of maryland had violated the 14th amendment's equal protection clause by providing in-state education to white students but not to black students. the state did not appeal the ruling to the us supreme court, so it was of limited applicability, but it was certainly an important milestone for the civil rights movement. in a determined effort to at least understand the navy's view of the situation, it is obvious that the service was caught in a vise of their own making. the stevedores at port chicago had scored at the nadir of the general classification test (the testing done by the military to determine the intelligence, comprehension, and aptitude of the millions of men who were conscripted or enlisted in the armed forces) and could justifiably be considered little more than strong backs by their superiors. during the forties, the testing was the best means available to assign personnel to the appropriate slot in the war machine. in later decades, after more ubiquitous uses of standardized testing, doubts regarding cultural bias would emerge and people would begin to question why such testing never included useful subjects like... the construction of a zip gun, for example. we may now consider such testing as hopelessly flawed, but it was the best and most objective tool available to the military at the time. somebody had to load munitions on ships and those who scored at the bottom of the gct were likely the ones least likely to harm the navy in its endeavors. given their poor scores, it was probably debatable whether they could have benefitted from specialized training in handling munitions. it was a bad situation with no real good possible outcome. given the situation, it seems likely that some sort of disaster was just waiting to rear its ugly head. the navy's viewpoint was both understandable and unforgivable. within a year of the war's end, all of the convicted "mutineers" had been released to service at sea. it took eighty years, but the navy finally exonerated each of the 258 men and closed the case that was such a stain on the navy's escutcheon. for us, it is important to realize that events of eighty years ago have little bearing on who we are today. it seems inconceivable that the us navy could have 100,000 black sailors yet not one black officer. yet, that was the case just eighty years ago. - sj
